newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil hopes for another record CS sugar crop.
newsitem.headline: Brazil hopes for another record CS sugar crop.

text.p: The prospects look sweet for the 1997/98 sugarcane crop in Brazil's center-south, with good weather conditions leading analysts to expect, if anything, a slightly larger crop than this year's record harvest.

"I think we are going to see a very good crop, better than this year. St. Peter has been very kind as the rains have been very beneficial and conditions are near to ideal," said Aloisio Sotero, analyst at consultants DataNet-AgriCommodities.
"Indications are the harvest should be of the same level as this year, maybe even a little bigger," said a spokesman from the Sao Paulo Sugar and Alcohol Association (AIAA).
The 1996/97 center-south crop which is mainly harvested between May and November reached 10.22 million tonnes according to DataNet's Sotero and 10.43 million, according to the AIAA.
The latter estimate is almost exactly within the crop plan published by the government in June last year which set a goal of 10.47 million tonnes for the region.
Within the plan, the government earmarked 3.68 million tonnes of sugar for export but this was increased by a further 500,000 tonnes in a decree published in December.

The additional quota has not yet however been exempted from a 40 percent export tax due to ongoing discussions between the Industry and Commerce and Finance Ministries as to how the extra allocations should be distributed amongst individual mills, a Finance Ministry spokesman said.
Analysts said one option that had been mooted was to reduce the quota to zero for specific regions but this was not seen as the most likely solution, the official said.
"The best solution is to reach agreement on a technical level as to how best to distribute the extra quotas," he added.
Pressure for additional tax-free export allowances has eased however with better domestic prices and lower external values and exports during January from the region have been muted.
Preliminary figures from Santos are of only 32,442 tonnes, no exports from Paranagua and 12,870 tonnes from Itajai, according to individual port authorities.
Analysts are already speculating the total liberation of sugar exports may soon be imminent, perhaps even this year.

Yesterday the head of the primary commodities department in the Industry and Commerce Ministry said the aim was to liberate the market at the same time as prices of hydrous alcohol are freed in May 1998.
But DataNet's Sotero said he believed the lifting of export quotas could even coincide with the liberalisation of anhydrous alcohol prices which is to take place this May.

Any concerns over how to ensure domestic supply of sugar and alcohol in a free market could be addressed by adopting a similar system as in the U.S. when the level of imports is regulated by a stocks to consumption ratio, he said.
In Brazil a mechanism could be devised using the relationship between domestic sugar and alcohol which could trigger the implementation of an export tax when necessary.
In the north/northeast where the harvest normally runs between September and April, there will be no need for extra export quotas this crop year, Sotero said.
Rather the region is likely to export substantially less than the 1.52 million tonnes set out in the crop plan, he said.
"I think exports from the north/northeast will be 20 percent less than anticipated," Sotero said.

"This is because the internal alcohol price is more attractive than the international sugar price. Also the January to March quarter is rainier than usual which is making grinding difficult," he added.
As a result, Sotero, who is based in Recife, said he now expected total sugar production in the region to be around three million tonnes against the 3.2 million tonnes included in the crop plan.
The harvest was also likely to end earlier with some 80 percent of factories expected to close by the first fortnight in March, Sotero said.
-- Rio de Janeiro newsroom, 5521 5074151
